Cut answers from the base and from RL have run out of search: they also finish with more tokens, but under a tenth are right. Ending a cut answer early by any means turns unfinished work into guesses that are right less often.

mechanisms.statement: A sample cut at the token cap gives no answer, so it casts no ballot in a vote. When a model's wrong attempts mostly end at the cap, the plurality is formed by right answers and the vote nears pass@k. Anything that turns cut attempts into finished answers (a larger cap, finishing directions, RL) adds wrong ballots. Those wrong ballots tie or outvote single right answers, so the vote gains less than the singles gain.

holds_against.why: The base gains 41 from voting on MATH-500 with few cap hits. There most problems have a right share above one half, so ballots are not the limit; abstention matters only where the right share is low, as on hard328 and fresh2026.
On fresh2026 the 1.5x edit (few cap hits) gains +4.75 from voting against RL's +6.5. That difference is inside the noise of n 136, and both gains stay far below Think-SFT's +15, which abstains most.

mechanisms.statement: Think-SFT was trained to end its reasoning at a </think> boundary and then write one short final answer and end-of-text. The raw template with the base's cue gives it no boundary, so after solving it keeps writing (re-checks, extra code blocks, new attempts) and stops late. In its own ChatML format it closes at the boundary: fewer answers reach 16k and output after the answer stops, with the same precision on finished answers.

holds_against.why: Think-SFT plain (raw template, no cue) scores 440 against 454 with the cue. That prompt has neither the cue nor the trained chat markers; the native template supplies <think>, the trained opening, so it is not the plain case.
In the raw template 91 of 93 cut answers do finish by 32k, so the model does stop eventually. The mechanism is about where it stops (at a trained boundary, earlier), not about whether it stops.

mechanisms.statement: RL's top directions shift the lm_head readout toward commit tokens (the box, end-of-text, the 'Okay' cue). The shift raises the per-token chance of ending at points where an answer is ready, and it scales with the edit's projection on that readout, not with its energy. Directions from Math, Code or IF that share the readout add up; random or Think-SFT directions add nothing. Subtracting the directions turns boxed endings into unboxed ones more than into cap hits.

holds_against.why: The 8 directions confined to layers 0-10 raise cap hits to 98. A partial layer band does not carry the readout projection that the full-depth directions write, so it is not a smaller dose of the same shift; the mechanism concerns whole-model direction sets.
Code's directions in layers 22-31 alone leave 34 cap hits. Again a band and not the whole set: the commit shift needs the earlier layers' input directions to fire at answer-ready points.

mechanisms.statement: Long Think-SFT traces can drift into a non-progress state: about 12-19 % of samples switch into Chinese connectives, with the median first switch near token 13,600. A drift entered before the cap rarely ends in a right answer, even with twice the tokens. The base and RL at T 1.0 neither loop nor drift. So the value of extra budget is lower where drift is common, and edits that shorten Think-SFT answers avoid mostly drift-bound attempts.

holds_against.why: Within a problem, a switch by token 8,000 changes the right rate by +5.3 points [-2, 13]. Early switches often revert (English resumes in 85 % of episodes); the harm is in late switches still in force at the cap (1 of 24 right versus 22 of 69).

The base's long answers finish right only 4 of 64 at 32k without any drift. Its cut answers fail for another reason (exhausted search); the mechanism does not claim drift is the only state that cannot be rescued.

mechanisms.statement: In the plain prompt the base's per-token chance of writing an 'Answer:' line and ending is high from the first few hundred tokens, so it stops before a derivation is done. The deliberative opening, chosen, prefilled or written by an edit, lowers that hazard for the whole answer. Lowering it is graded, not a switch: accuracy follows how far the hazard drops, and early stops cost only on problems that need length.

holds_against.why: Plain draws that do not open with 'Okay' score 216, the plain level; selecting the opening gives the whole gain. The opening sets the end hazard for the rest of the answer, so a chosen opening lowers it everywhere, which this mechanism expects.
Short top-8 answers are right 82.9 % of the time. They sit on easy problems the base solves 4 of 4, where an early end costs nothing; the mechanism puts the loss on problems that need length.
